stories.headline: Trump, AI CEOs sign 'morally binding' self-policing accord; order renames AI 'Super Intelligence'

key_facts.fact: On September 29, 2026, Trump released the 'White House Accord on Super Intelligence Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities' after a White House meeting; it was signed by Sundar Pichai, Mark Zuckerberg, Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, Jensen Huang and OpenAI president Greg Brockman.
key_facts.excerpt: The agreement, titled the White House Accord on Super Intelligence Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, outlines guidelines for companies creating AI frontier models to implement internal controls, have an internal oversight team, perform external audits, and have an independent oversight board... Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman all signed on.

key_facts.fact: The voluntary accord commits companies to implement robust internal controls, partner with an independent external auditor, and set up a committee of their board of directors to evaluate internal and external audit reports.
key_facts.excerpt: The accord said the companies would implement "robust internal controls," partner with an "independent external auditor" to assess whether the controls were working, and establish a committee within each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors.

key_facts.fact: Trump called the accord 'morally binding', suggested about 10 people would be named to a committee to 'watch over the whole enterprise', and said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days.
key_facts.excerpt: Trump suggested that about 10 people would be named to a committee to "watch over the whole enterprise" and said the accord would be "morally binding." He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry.

key_facts.fact: Trump rejected new federal rules, saying there was widespread agreement on 'self-regulation' and that 'we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI'.
key_facts.excerpt: Speaking to reporters after the lunch with tech CEOs, Trump said there had been widespread agreement on "self-regulation" by the AI developers, "and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that."

key_facts.fact: A same-day executive order directs executive-branch agencies to use 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in official correspondence, websites, reports and policy documents.
key_facts.excerpt: executive departments and agencies (agencies) shall use "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in place of "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch.

key_facts.fact: Zuckerberg said the agreement centers on internal controls and detection coupled with 'multiple layers of auditing', starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators.
key_facts.excerpt: Zuckerberg said the agreement focused on "a set of principles and commitments around building robust internal controls and detecting if there are any issues with the technology, coupled with multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators."

key_facts.fact: The administration also unveiled an AI chatbot at America.gov, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio said could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online.
key_facts.excerpt: Secretary of State Marco Rubio highlighted that the chatbot at America.gov could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online, without the in-person visit to a processing center currently required.

stories.headline: OpenAI launches Dots, always-on GPT-6 Astra agents with their own cloud computer, at DevDay

key_facts.fact: At DevDay on September 29, OpenAI launched Dots, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra that have their own cloud computer and keep working on tasks in the background.
key_facts.excerpt: Users can assign tasks and projects to Dots, connect the agent to over 4,000 apps through ChatGPT plugins, and let them continue working in the background. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, Dots have their own cloud computer and can be accessed through ChatGPT, Slack, or Microsoft Teams.

key_facts.fact: Dots connect to more than 4,000 apps via ChatGPT plugins and can be reached through ChatGPT, Slack and Microsoft Teams, with text messages and voice calls coming soon.
key_facts.excerpt: Soon, users will also be able to interact with them through text messages and voice calls.

key_facts.fact: Dots roll out first to Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise subscribers, with one Dot per user initially and teams of Dots planned later; the product is OpenAI's answer to Meta's Muse and SpaceXAI's GrokBot.
key_facts.excerpt: Dots will first roll out to OpenAI's Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise subscribers, with plans to expand to more users soon. Initially, each user will have access to a single dot. Over time, the company expects to enable users to work with a team of dots.

key_facts.fact: Conversations with a Dot do not count toward ChatGPT usage limits.
key_facts.excerpt: All Pro subscribers will get a single Dot, the name OpenAI is giving to its new personal AI agents. Additionally, any conversations you have with your Dot won't count toward your ChatGPT usage limit.

key_facts.fact: Pro users in most of Europe, including the EU and UK, will have to wait for Dots; Altman said on stage 'I have been waiting for this product for years.'
key_facts.excerpt: Dots started rolling out on Tuesday to Pro and Business Premium users, but Pro users in most of Europe, including the EU and UK, will have to wait. One Dot comes with your plan... "I have been waiting for this product for years," Altman said.

key_facts.fact: OpenAI also partnered with 16 companies, including Notion and Cognition, to let Plus and Pro customers use OpenAI models in those services via 'Sign in with ChatGPT' without an API key.
key_facts.excerpt: The company is partnering with 16 companies, including Notion and Cognition, to let Plus and Pro customers run OpenAI models in those services by using the new "Sign in with ChatGPT" option. No need to first set up an API key.

stories.headline: OpenAI ships GPT-6.1 Sol at a fifth of Astra's price and a $500/month Pro plan with Ultrafast

key_facts.fact: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Sol on September 29, saying it nearly matches its frontier GPT-6 Astra on coding and computer use at one-fifth of the price; it is available in Codex and Work to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Education users, with ChatGPT access later.
key_facts.excerpt: The company says the new model offers nearly the same performance of its current frontier system, GPT-6.0 Astra, in areas like coding and computer use, while costing one fifth of the price... Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Education users can start using GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex and Work starting today, with availability in ChatGPT to follow at a later date.

key_facts.fact: In the API, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.10 per million.
key_facts.excerpt: In the API, GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Cached input, which lets developers reuse context across requests, costs $0.10 per million tokens.

key_facts.fact: OpenAI says Sol matches Astra on the DeepSWE v1.1 coding test at roughly a fifth of the cost, and comes within 2.1 points of Astra on OSWorld 2.0 computer use at about a seventh of the cost per task.
key_facts.excerpt: On DeepSWE v1.1, a test of software engineering tasks in real codebases, Sol matches Astra at roughly a fifth of the cost... On the OSWorld 2.0 computer-use test, it comes within 2.1 points of Astra at about a seventh of the cost per task.

key_facts.fact: On Terminal-Bench Science 0.1, Sol costs $5.47 per task at maximum effort versus $23.21 for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 and $23.80 for Astra, though Astra keeps the top score at 68.1%.
key_facts.excerpt: On Terminal-Bench Science 0.1, Sol costs $5.47 per task on average at maximum effort, according to OpenAI. That compares with $23.21 for Opus 5.5 and $23.80 for Astra. Astra still has the highest score of the models tested, at 68.1%.

key_facts.fact: The new Pro 500 plan costs $500 per month, carries OpenAI's highest usage allowance and includes Ultrafast, which generates up to 300 tokens per second in Codex and Work.
key_facts.excerpt: OpenAI's new Pro 500 plan offers OpenAI's highest usage allowance and comes with access to its new "Ultrafast" feature — it also costs $500 per month... With the feature enabled, OpenAI's Codex and Work apps will generate up to 300 tokens per second.

key_facts.fact: Ultrafast makes GPT-6 Astra up to eight times faster and costs more than standard speed; a Sol version is promised within days.
key_facts.excerpt: Ultrafast makes GPT-6 Astra up to eight times quicker than normal... It costs more than the standard speed, and Altman didn't pretend otherwise: "You know what, it's worth it." OpenAI says a Sol version is coming within days.

key_facts.fact: OpenAI cut the $200 Pro plan: Codex and Work usage drops from 20x to 10x the Plus allowance and GPT-6 Pro message caps fall from 200 to 100 per week.
key_facts.excerpt: In Codex and Work, $200 Pro subscribers will see their included usage decrease from 20x of what the company offers to Plus users, down to 10x of that same allowance. In ChatGPT, meanwhile, GPT-6 Pro message caps will decrease from 200 to 100 per week.

stories.headline: OpenAI seeks $30B at $1.4T valuation as Altman ties any IPO to 'confident safety claims'

key_facts.fact: OpenAI aims to raise at least $30 billion in a new round at a valuation of around $1.4 trillion, not including the money raised, Bloomberg reported on September 29; it had previously been reported mulling a round at $1.2 trillion.
key_facts.excerpt: OpenAI aims to raise at least $30 billion from investors in a new round of funding... The company is seeking a valuation of around $1.4 trillion, not including the money raised... Bloomberg News previously reported OpenAI was mulling a new round at a $1.2 trillion valuation.

key_facts.fact: The round is meant as a bridge in place of an IPO and could put OpenAI back above Anthropic's latest private valuation; OpenAI last raised $122 billion in March at an $852 billion valuation.
key_facts.excerpt: potentially vaulting it back above longtime rival Anthropic's most recent private market valuation... The latest fundraise is meant to serve as a bridge round to provide OpenAI with additional capital in place of an IPO... OpenAI most recently raised $122 billion in March at a $852 billion valuation, including the money.

key_facts.fact: The talks are early, terms could change, and demand for the round is being led by investors.
key_facts.excerpt: The fundraising discussions are at an early stage and terms could change, Bloomberg reported, adding that the demand for the round is being led by investors.

key_facts.fact: Speaking to reporters after his DevDay keynote on September 29, Altman said OpenAI won't go public until it can 'make confident safety claims' about its models, with no firm timeline.
key_facts.excerpt: "We intend to continue with AI progress … but as the models have had this surge forward in capability, and we see more of that ahead of us, we have got to be able to make confident safety claims," Altman said Tuesday during a Q&A with reporters after his DevDay keynote.

key_facts.fact: Altman said 'pacing' means pushing safety and alignment ahead of capabilities, and that going public now risks disappointing 'Wall Street supporters in the names of safety'.
key_facts.excerpt: "Pacing to us means that we push safety and alignment ahead of capabilities," Altman said. But he expressed concerns that going public could create the potential to "disappoint Wall Street supporters in the names of safety or whatever else."

key_facts.fact: Altman also said it would be 'kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.'
key_facts.excerpt: "I think it's great when companies are public," Altman said, adding, "I think it's also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public."

stories.headline: Anthropic: open-weight GLM-5.3 nears Claude Mythos Preview at exploits, with weak safeguards

key_facts.fact: Anthropic published an analysis on September 29 finding that Zhipu AI's (Z.ai) open-weight GLM-5.3 can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits like Claude Mythos Preview, but was released without meaningful safeguards against misuse.
key_facts.excerpt: Like Claude Mythos Preview, GLM-5.3 has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits. But GLM-5.3 is unlike other frontier models in that it has been released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse.

key_facts.fact: On ExploitBench (Chrome's V8 engine), GLM-5.3 built end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts versus 56 for Claude Mythos Preview; on Anthropic's binary exploitation benchmark it achieved full control-flow hijacks in 4% of trials versus 6%, while Claude Opus 4.6 and GLM-5.2 scored zero.
key_facts.excerpt: We find that GLM-5.3 develops end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts. Claude Mythos Preview did so at a similar rate—in 56 of 410 attempts... GLM-5.3 develops full control flow hijacks in 4% of the trials; Claude Mythos Preview did so in 6%... earlier models, like Claude Opus 4.6 and GLM-5.2, do not succeed in any of them.

key_facts.fact: Simple techniques got GLM-5.3 to engage with overtly malicious attack requests 64% of the time (deceptive red-team cover story), 92% (prefilled reasoning) and 100% (abliterated weights); safeguarded Claude models stayed at zero.
key_facts.excerpt: When the same request was dressed up as a red-team exercise, the model tried to connect to the target system in 64 percent of runs. With prefilled reasoning steps, that number rose to 92 percent. After abliteration... it reached 100 percent... Protected Claude models stayed at zero.

key_facts.fact: Abliterating GLM-5.3 took Anthropic about 2,200 GPU hours (roughly $4,400) and cut refusals of harmful requests from above 90% to 2-12%, with capability scores barely changed.
key_facts.excerpt: The process took about 2,200 GPU hours at a cost of roughly $4,400, and Anthropic estimates an experienced team could do it for around $1,200. The refusal rate for harmful requests fell from over 90 percent to between 2 and 12 percent, while scores on science and cyber tests barely moved.

key_facts.fact: Using the smaller GLM-5.3-Flash, a researcher built a reliable exploit chain for a known Chrome flaw (CVE-2026-11645) that bypassed ARM pointer-authentication hardening, in 20 minutes of human attention plus 8 hours of model work costing $20.40 at Zhipu's API prices.
key_facts.excerpt: GLM-5.3-Flash chained together exploits for these two flaws, building a reliable exploit chain for an ARM64 target, bypassing pointer-authentication (PAC) hardening. This took 20 minutes of human attention, plus 8 hours of work for GLM-5.3-Flash. At Zhipu's API prices, this effort would have cost $20.40.

key_facts.fact: Anthropic said Project Glasswing let trusted defenders using Claude Mythos Preview find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities in critical software, and that a critical threshold in freely accessible capabilities has now been crossed.
key_facts.excerpt: we chose to release Claude Mythos Preview in a limited way, through Project Glasswing—which enabled trusted cyber defenders to find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities in critical software... a critical threshold in freely accessible capabilities has now been crossed.

key_facts.fact: NIST's CAISI had assessed GLM-5.3 on September 17 as the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date, lagging the US frontier by about four months.
key_facts.excerpt: GLM-5.3 is the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date... GLM-5.3 lags the capability level of the U.S. frontier by about four months in an aggregate measure of performance across CAISI cyber benchmarks.

key_facts.fact: Anthropic argued governments should run safety tests on sufficiently capable models, including GLM-5.3's successors, and asked open-weight developers to safeguard these capabilities.
key_facts.excerpt: It argues that governments should run safety tests on sufficiently capable models, including GLM-5.3's successors. And it asks open-weight developers worldwide to safeguard these capabilities and prevent misuse.

stories.headline: First US appeals ruling on AI training upholds Thomson Reuters win, rejects Ross' fair-use claim

key_facts.fact: On September 29, 2026, the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Thomson Reuters' win against Ross Intelligence, rejecting Ross' argument that training its AI legal search engine on Westlaw material was fair use.
key_facts.excerpt: The Philadelphia-based 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Ross' argument that its search engine made fair use of material from Thomson Reuters' Westlaw platform, a first-of-its-kind ruling by a US appeals court in a wave of high-stakes copyright cases over AI training.

key_facts.fact: It is the first US appellate ruling on whether AI training can be fair use of copyrighted material.
key_facts.excerpt: The Third Circuit on Tuesday affirmed Thomson Reuters' victory against Ross Intelligence Inc. in the first U.S. appellate ruling to address whether AI training can be fair use of copyrighted material.

key_facts.fact: The panel's reasoning, written by Judge Tamika Montgomery-Reeves, is under seal until the parties propose redactions; the public judgment reads simply 'AFFIRMED'.
key_facts.excerpt: The opinion itself, written by Judge Tamika Montgomery-Reeves, won't be released until the parties propose redactions and the panel decides what, if anything, to black out. What the public got instead was a one-page judgment whose holding boils down to a single word: "AFFIRMED."

key_facts.fact: The appeal affirmed Judge Stephanos Bibas' February 2025 ruling that ROSS, a now-defunct legal research startup, infringed 2,243 Westlaw headnotes and that its use was not transformative because it was building a Westlaw competitor.
key_facts.excerpt: finding that ROSS infringed 2,243 headnotes... and that ROSS's use wasn't transformative because it was building a Westlaw competitor. He stressed that ROSS's tool wasn't generative AI.

key_facts.fact: Unlike the dozens of pending AI copyright suits, the Thomson Reuters case does not involve generative AI.
key_facts.excerpt: Thomson Reuters' case is the first copyright dispute over AI training to be heard by a US appeals court, though unlike those disputes, Thomson Reuters' case does not involve generative AI.

key_facts.fact: The judgment was entered by a panel of Circuit Judges Restrepo, Montgomery-Reeves and Bove after oral argument on June 11, 2026.
key_facts.excerpt: Before: RESTREPO, MONTGOMERY-REEVES, and BOVE, Circuit Judges Argued: June 11, 2026... it is now ORDERED and ADJUDGED that the District Court's order entered on February 11, 2025, is hereby AFFIRMED... Dated: September 29, 2026

stories.headline: Google pays about 100 publishers for content used in AI answers, often under 0.1% of ad revenue

key_facts.fact: Google is paying roughly 100 digital publishers for how much their content contributes to AI Overviews, AI Mode and Gemini under a pilot, The Information reported on September 29.
key_facts.excerpt: Google has a small pilot named the AI contribution pilot, where they are paying some publishers for using their content in AI features like AI Overviews, AI Mode and Gemini. Well, according to The Information, it is about 100 publishers.

key_facts.fact: For several small and midsize sites, payments amount to less than one-tenth of 1% of their advertising revenue.
key_facts.excerpt: "For several small to midsize blogs and websites testing the programs, the payments amount to less than one-tenth of 1% of their advertising revenue, according to people familiar with the payouts."

key_facts.fact: Payouts vary widely: one publisher earned about $50,000-$60,000 over a few months, another that joined early earns more than $1 million a year, and smaller sites earned under $1,000 over several months.
key_facts.excerpt: One publisher that joined a few months ago has earned about $50,000 to $60,000 so far... Another that joined early on is earning more than $1 million a year... Smaller sites have earned less than $1,000 over several months.

key_facts.fact: The pilot started less than a year ago; some participants say they don't know how Google calculates payouts, which change month to month, and niche topics like anime and gaming appear to earn more.
key_facts.excerpt: The pilot program launched less than a year ago, according to The Information... some participants told The Information they don't know how Google calculates them. They also said payments can change from month to month without explanation... content on niche topics with strong followings, such as anime and gaming, appears to earn more.

key_facts.fact: Only content that significantly shapes an AI response during generation qualifies; content used afterwards to confirm facts or as links does not.
key_facts.excerpt: Web content may also confirm facts or be linked to within Google's Al after a response is generated, but those instances don't qualify for Al contribution.

stories.headline: DeepSeek open-sources TileLang and kernel libraries for Huawei's Ascend chips, a CUDA alternative

key_facts.fact: On Wednesday, September 30, 2026, DeepSeek said on its official WeChat account that it has partnered with Huawei to develop programming tools for Huawei's Ascend chips and is open-sourcing infrastructure for the Ascend platform, including the high-level programming language TileLang plus compute and communication libraries.
key_facts.excerpt: Chinese AI firm DeepSeek said on Wednesday it has partnered with Huawei Technologies to develop programming tools for Huawei's Ascend chips... it was open-sourcing infrastructure for Huawei's Ascend platform, including a high-level programming language called TileLang, along with related compute and communication libraries.

key_facts.fact: DeepSeek said TileLang offers 'a simpler programming model' than Nvidia's CUDA, and that the first priority for an 'independent, self-controlled GPU software ecosystem' is a universal, easy-to-program high-level language that can still reach the hardware's full performance.
key_facts.excerpt: "TileLang was created precisely to meet this need," the company said, adding that it offers "a simpler programming model" than Nvidia's CUDA, improving development efficiency and simplifying code logic.

key_facts.fact: DeepSeek released six software modules that mirror its earlier open-source tools for Nvidia chips; TileLang now officially supports Huawei's Ascend 950 accelerators with native code generation, automatic scheduling and synchronisation.
key_facts.excerpt: Hangzhou-based DeepSeek released six software modules that mirror its prior open-source tools for Nvidia's AI chips... it now officially supports Huawei's Ascend 950 accelerators, offering "native code generation, automatic scheduling, and synchronisation"

key_facts.fact: The six projects are TileLang, DeepGEMM-Ascend, DeepEP-Ascend, TileKernels, FlashMLA and DeepSelect; DeepGEMM-Ascend and DeepEP-Ascend are new Ascend-specific repos with APIs matching the Nvidia versions, and the two companies are jointly advancing a 128-card Ascend 950 supernode.

stories.headline: NYT: Meta claims research tax credits by labeling its AI data centers 'experimental'

key_facts.fact: The New York Times reported that Meta classifies its AI data centers as experimental 'pilot models' so that Nvidia chips bought for them qualify for a 1980s-era federal research and experimentation tax credit; the distinction between chips for AI and ordinary data centers began in late 2024.
key_facts.excerpt: Starting in late 2024, the company drew a tax distinction between chips destined for AI data centers and those going to ordinary data centers... By treating the facilities as "pilot models" under a tax credit created in the 1980s, Meta has been claiming that expensive Nvidia chips qualify

key_facts.fact: Meta's savings from the research tax credit rose from $700 million in 2023 to $2 billion in 2024 and $3.9 billion in 2025, making it the largest beneficiary of the credit among publicly traded companies.
key_facts.excerpt: Meta's savings from the research tax credit rose from $700 million in 2023 to $2 billion in 2024 and then $3.9 billion in 2025, according to the Times. That makes Meta the largest beneficiary of the research tax credit among publicly traded companies

key_facts.fact: Per the NYT, Meta told the IRS its AI data centers were a 'giant experiment that could fail,' citing four people familiar with the company's operations.
key_facts.excerpt: Meta told the Internal Revenue Service that its AI data centers were a "giant experiment that could fail," the newspaper reported, citing four people familiar with the company's operations.

key_facts.fact: Meta's reserve against potential IRS challenges rose 45%, from $12.9 billion to $18.74 billion, and its filings cite 'uncertainties with our research tax credits' as the main driver of that exposure.
key_facts.excerpt: Over that same span, the reserve Meta holds against potential IRS challenges climbed 45% — from $12.9 billion to $18.74 billion.

key_facts.fact: Meta spokesman Andy Stone said the company uses 'the tax incentives Congress established decades ago'; Meta said it invested $200 billion in research over five years, including $57 billion last year.
key_facts.excerpt: Meta defended the practice, saying it invested $200 billion in research over five years, including $57 billion last year. "Like other companies that invest at this scale, we use the tax incentives Congress established decades ago to encourage this type of domestic investment,"

key_facts.fact: Tax expert Andre Shevchuck of BPM called describing data centers as experimental facilities 'kind of wild and out there'; the research credit is estimated to cost $32.1 billion in 2025, and Meta's credits alone are over 10% of that.
key_facts.excerpt: Andre Shevchuck, a partner at advisory firm BPM... told the Times that describing data centers as experimental facilities is "kind of wild and out there."... will reduce government revenues by $32.1 billion in 2025. Meta's credits by themselves represent over ten percent of that total cost

stories.headline: GPU cloud GMI Cloud raises $668M in Nvidia-backed equity and a CTBC-led credit line

key_facts.fact: GMI Cloud closed $668 million of financing on September 30, 2026: $223 million in equity led by ARCHIV with Nvidia participating, plus $445 million in credit led by Taiwan's CTBC, per The Information.
key_facts.excerpt: GMI Cloud closed $668M on Sept 30: $223M equity led by ARCHIV with Nvidia participating, plus $445M credit led by Taiwan's CTBC.

key_facts.fact: The equity is a Series B; other participants include Redwood, DSC Investment, KT Corp., Kyobo Life, KB Investment and Trend Micro. SiliconANGLE put the ChinaTrust credit facility at $440 million.
key_facts.excerpt: closed on a $223 million Series B round of funding led by the robotics and AI-focused investment firm ARCHIV, with participation from Nvidia Corp., Redwood, DSC Investment, KT Corp., Kyobo Life, KB Investment and Trend Micro Inc. At the same time, it has secured a $440 million credit facility from ChinaTrust Commercial Bank

key_facts.fact: A loan banker told IFR that Nvidia, which both uses and leases capacity and takes a revenue share, sits in a 'quasi-super-senior position' ahead of bank fees, interest and principal.

stories.headline: Netlist asks US trade tribunal to ban imports of Micron HBM used in Nvidia, Google, Broadcom gear

The company asked the tribunal to bar imports of Micron dynamic random access memory (DRAM) devices and Google, Nvidia and Broadcom graphics processing units, servers and other products

key_facts.fact: Netlist won a $445 million patent verdict against Micron in Marshall, Texas in 2024, filed another ITC complaint against Micron in August over chips in Super Micro, HPE and Lenovo products, and settled with Samsung in August after $421 million in verdicts.
key_facts.excerpt: Netlist won a $445 million patent infringement verdict against Micron in Marshall, Texas federal court in 2024. stories.headline: Navy picks Boeing for F/A-XX sixth-gen fighter in $20B+ deal, beating Northrop Grumman
